newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues First California over municipal bonds.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues First California over municipal bonds.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday sued underwriter First California Capital Markets Group Inc, capping a three-year municipal bond probe that has divided the public finance community.
The SEC said it sued First California and two of its executives for allegedly defrauding investors who bought $69 million of bonds in five California municipal offerings.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, alleged that First California principal H. Michael Richardson and former manager Derrick Dumont lied to municipal bond investors and omitted important information from bond offering documents about the risks investors faced.

The six-count complaint asks the court to order them to return "all ill-gotten gains" plus interest and to pay civil penalties. The SEC also asked the court to prevent the defendants from violating securities laws in the future.
If the SEC is successful, First California and its executives could be forced to pay more than $1 million.
First California and its attorneys were not immediately available to comment.

For nearly three years the SEC has been investigating First California deals in Nevada County and in the cities of Ione, Avenal and Wasco. The bonds were issued under California's complex Marks-Roos and Mello-Roos bond rules.

The Marks-Roos Local Bond Pooling Act allows local governments to form joint authorities that issue bonds to finance capital projects. The Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act allows local governments to finance a variety of local facilities and services with bonds supported by special taxes.
Both bonding acts have come under fire in recent years because many of the deals have experienced financial trouble, including those underwritten by First California.

The SEC alleged that official statements for the Nevada County and Ione bonds contained misrepresentations and omissions that were important to investors because they made the projects and the bonds seem less risky than they actually were.
The SEC also alleged that First California and Richardson lied to investors and omitted important information in official statements for the Avenal and Wasco bonds.

David Bayless, the SEC's district administrator in San Francisco, said the First California lawsuit should send a message to other bond professionals that the commission is committed to "cleaning up the municipal securities market."
"By bringing this action against an underwriter, I think the commission is sending this message loud and clear," Bayless said.
The First California case attracted national attention because it was one of the SEC's first municipal bond investigations to target local governments.
The case sparked a heated debate in the municipal finance community over who should be held responsible when bond deals go bad.
SEC critics argue that local government officials are not sophisticated bond professionals and should not be held liable for complex transactions they do not understand.
Others say local elected officials need to spend more time reviewing bond deals and should be held accountable along with the bond professionals they hired.
For their part, Nevada County, Ione, Avenal and Wasco officials have denied any wrongdoing, insisting they relied on municipal bond professionals to prepare and sell the bonds.
